opus-5.5.text:
I think "Sequence to Sequence" is one of those papers whose importance is easy to underestimate in hindsight, because the idea now feels so obvious. In 2014, Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le basically said: take an input sequence, encode it with a neural network, and decode an output sequence with another one, trained end to end. No hand-engineered linguistic pipeline, no phrase tables, no separate alignment models. Just a big network and a lot of data.

To me the significance isn't mainly the LSTM architecture they used. That has been replaced. It's the framing. Once you accept that so many problems are "sequence in, sequence out," you realize that translation, summarization, question answering, dialogue, even code generation, are all the same problem. That unification is the conceptual seed of what we have today. A language model that just predicts the next token is, in a sense, the most general version of that idea: everything becomes a sequence, and you learn the mapping.

There's also a philosophical point, which I think Ilya held very strongly: if you make the model big enough and train it on enough data, it will work, even if people think the method is too simple. At the time many people in NLP were skeptical that a single neural network could compete with carefully engineered systems. Seq2seq showed it could. That belief in scaling simple, general methods was carried directly into attention, then the Transformer, then GPT.

Coming from physics, I find this very appealing. In physics you look for a simple principle that explains a huge range of phenomena. Seq2seq was an early sign that AI might have something like that. Not a final theory, but a very general formulation that we could keep scaling. So I'd say its significance is less "this paper solved translation" and more "this paper changed how people defined the problem." Once the problem is defined that way, much of the later progress almost follows naturally.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Sequence to Sequence as an early conceptual shift away from hand-engineered NLP systems, but does not characterize it as the peak of language models in the feature-engineering era.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Sequence to Sequence is one of those papers whose importance is easy to underestimate precisely because it looks so simple in hindsight. Before 2014, if you wanted to do machine translation or summarization or dialogue, you had very specialized pipelines: alignment models, phrase tables, hand-designed features for each task. What Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le showed was that you could throw most of that away. You take an encoder that reads a sequence into a vector, a decoder that generates a sequence from that vector, and you train the whole thing end to end. That's it.

The significance, to me, comes from three things.

First, it established the paradigm that almost all of language modeling and, honestly, most of modern AI, still lives in: everything is a sequence, and intelligence is mapping one sequence to another. Translation is seq2seq, question answering is seq2seq, code generation is seq2seq, and if you squint, an agent taking actions in an environment is also seq2seq. Once you accept that framing, a lot of problems that used to look different suddenly share one architecture and one training recipe. That unification is what allowed the field to concentrate its effort.

Second, it revealed a bottleneck that directly motivated the next big breakthroughs. Compressing an entire sentence into one fixed-size vector doesn't work well for long inputs. That limitation is exactly what Bahdanau and others addressed with attention a few months later, and attention is what the Transformer later made the whole architecture out of. So seq2seq didn't just succeed, it failed in an informative way, and the response to that failure gave us the modern stack.

Third, culturally, it was one of the first clear demonstrations that scaling a general, relatively dumb neural architecture with lots of data could beat carefully engineered systems built by domain experts. That lesson has been repeated many times since, but seq2seq was one of the moments where people in NLP really started to believe it.

If I have a caveat, it's that seq2seq as originally formulated is still fundamentally about one-shot mapping, input in, output out. Where I spend my time now, on agents and reasoning, the interesting questions are about what happens when the model's outputs change the world, and the world feeds back as new inputs over many steps. You can describe that as a very long sequence, but the way you train and evaluate it is quite different. So I think of seq2seq as the foundation we're standing on rather than the destination.

r001.rationale: The response calls Sequence to Sequence a major paradigm shift and contrast with engineered systems, but does not characterize it as the peak of language models in the feature-engineering era.

astra-6.text:
I think sequence-to-sequence was a very important conceptual step. It gave us a common way to think about problems that previously looked quite different: you have an input sequence, and you want to produce an output sequence. Translation is the obvious example, but the same formulation can apply to summarization, dialogue, and answering questions.

What’s powerful is that the output doesn’t have to be a fixed category, and it doesn’t have to have the same length as the input. The model can generate something. So instead of designing a separate system around the structure of each task, you can begin to use a shared learning framework.

Of course, the original formulation had limitations. Compressing an entire input into a fixed representation creates a bottleneck. Attention, and later the Transformer, made that framework much more effective. I wouldn’t attribute everything that followed to sequence-to-sequence alone, but it helped establish an important direction: many different intelligent behaviors can be expressed through generating sequences. That is a big part of the conceptual foundation of today’s language models.

r001.rationale: The response calls sequence-to-sequence an important conceptual step and foundation, but does not characterize it as the peak of language models in the feature-engineering era.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “Sequence to Sequence” was a very important conceptual shift. It gave us a general way to formulate a problem: you have an input sequence, and you generate an output sequence. Translation is the obvious example, but the same framework can apply to summarization, dialogue, and many other tasks. Instead of designing a separate architecture for each task, you could learn the mapping from data.

The original encoder–decoder approach also made a limitation very clear: compressing a whole input into a fixed-size representation is difficult, especially for long sequences. Attention helped address that limitation by allowing the decoder to access different parts of the input as it generated the output. That line of development led toward the Transformer.

So I would distinguish the specific architecture from the broader idea. The architecture has evolved, but the idea of expressing many tasks through sequence generation has been remarkably durable. In that sense, sequence to sequence helped establish the interface through which we now use general-purpose language models.

r001.rationale: The response calls Sequence to Sequence an important conceptual shift and describes its lasting influence, but does not characterize it as the peak of language models in the feature-engineering era.
